title_en: How much more air can come out of the AI trade?
Patients may miss out on NHS weight-loss jabs in England after GP funding withdrawn
excerpt_en: Inquiry finds most integrated care boards have scrapped payments to GPs for prescribing and monitoring the drug
body_en: Patients who are eligible for potentially life-changing weight-loss injections on the NHS risk missing out after most integrated care boards (ICBs) in England withdrew funding for GP services, an investigation has found.

The inquiry, conducted by the GP magazine Pulse, found that 21 of 36 ICBs have scrapped payments to practices for prescribing and monitoring Mounjaro, also known as tirzepatide. A further nine never had a local enhanced service and only four still retain one.

Although NHS England said funding was now national, with incentives for GPs to manage obesity added to the Quality and Outcomes Framework from April, the scheme is voluntary. GPs told Pulse the payments were not enough to cover the cost of providing the service.
Chris McCann, the acting chief executive of Healthwatch England, said patients had reported significant differences in their ability to obtain NHS-funded weight-loss drugs.

“Many people describe a postcode lottery in access to NHS-funded weight-loss drugs,” he said. “Depending on where they live, people can face very different routes to getting the medication, and in some areas access remains unclear while local commissioning arrangements are still being decided.”

In some areas of England, NHS bosses have already warned patients that the prescribing of Mounjaro cannot be guaranteed. Cheshire and Merseyside ICB, for example, states that GP participation is optional and that meeting the eligibility criteria does not guarantee access.

Since GPs were able to begin prescribing Mounjaro in 2025, access to the weight-loss medication has been reported to be a postcode lottery across England. The Guardian reported last year that thousands of patients in England were unable to access weight-loss jabs through their GP, with only 18 of 42 commissioning bodies having confirmed they had begun prescribing the drug.

The British Medical Association said the new payments were unlikely to cover the extra work involved in prescribing and monitoring the drug and that eligible patients were missing out as a result. It said the arrangements could become increasingly unsustainable as the NHS widens eligibility to more people over the coming years.

Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, the president of the Royal College of GPs, also raised concerns, saying the college recognised the worry that the new arrangements “may not adequately support the clinical work involved in assessing patients, prescribing safely and providing ongoing monitoring and follow-up”.

She added: “It is vital that general practice is appropriately supported to deliver safe, high-quality care as part of any additional responsibilities associated with the rollout of weight-loss drugs in the NHS.”
Related: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears

Prof Andy Brooks, the clinical chair of the National Association of Primary Care, said people eligible for tirzepatide needed “a clear, properly resourced route to treatment and follow-up”, including continuity of care for those already taking it.

He added: “This illustrates the limits of paying for individual activities for complex problems, which require a far more coordinated approach. We should start with the needs of our populations and the outcomes that matter to people, bringing together neighbourhood partners to plan and properly resource prevention, weight management support and treatment.
“The test is whether people can get the support they need when they need it, whether inequities in access narrow and whether that support can be sustained.”

NHS England said: “The NHS has moved funding for tirzepatide support into the GP contract, replacing varied local arrangements with a clear, nationally funded approach. This gives practices a consistent framework to support eligible patients and helps improve equitable access across the country.”

title_en: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
excerpt_en: Co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia, which is exporting climate pain
body_en: The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multiculturalism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.
Related: Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable

Governments have spent the past 35 years negotiating the global response to preventing “dangerous interference” with the climate system. Over that same period global warming has increased to close to 1.4C, with observed warming now accelerating above 0.3C per decade. Now, we’re facing an imminent breach of the Paris agreement’s critical 1.5C warming limit.
Successive Australian governments have either actively denied the problem exists – or have talked loud and long about how they are playing their role.

And what a role it has been! Australia’s coal exports have tripled since 1991; LNG exports have increased 20-fold. Australia now contributes about 4.3% of global fossil carbon emissions through both its domestic activities, and as the third-largest exporter of fossil fuels of all time.

Now that Australia’s efforts to host successful climate talks have failed so badly to deliver at a global level, we must turn to the urgent question: what will the government deliver for Australians at home?

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has called the current decade “critical” for combating climate change. He told leaders at Cop31 they had a “solemn responsibility” to act – and he’s said that every fraction of a degree of warming prevented matters.

If anyone needed confirmation of that during the past year, they only needed to turn on the TV news or, in some cases, to walk out of their house. From Adelaide to Sydney, the south-east broiled in January. Bush burned, homes ignited, lungs filled with smoke. Can you guess what made the heat so brutal? And the floods so powerful?

Further afield, in countries that gave the Australian colony many of its people, things were equally desperate. Italy, Greece, Britain, Spain … all of Europe crackled through its summer, leaving an estimated 50,000 people dead before their time.

South and east Asia (many of them our LNG markets) shared the pain, with temperatures hitting a close-to-unliveable 52C in Pakistan. All of it driven by climate change; all of it driven by burning fossil fuels.

So that’s the logical framing when you hear government ministers from the prime minister down celebrating new fossil fuel finds, talking about how the country benefits from extracting and exporting coal, oil and gas.
In Australia’s approvals pipeline are four 'carbon bombs', defined by scientists as projects that could emit a billion or more tonnes of fossil CO2

The government clearly didn’t turn on the TV news nor leave its house this year: it was too busy planning for coal and gas exports staying close to present levels over the next decade, at exactly the time emissions globally should be halving.

In Australia’s approvals pipeline are four “carbon bombs”, defined by scientists as projects that could emit a billion or more tonnes of fossil CO2. Off the coast of Western Australia there’s the Browse gas development at the pristine Scott Reef, the Valhalla fracking project in WA’s Kimberley further north, the Beetaloo basin fracking project in the Northern Territory, and the massive Hunter Valley Operations coalmine in New South Wales.
Albanese’s ministers have shown little other than full-blooded support for these projects going ahead. Is it no wonder then that we left Antalya with no agreement?

Rather than a decision to build on the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) roadmap initiated by Brazil, the only reference to fossil fuels remaining in the final text offered by Turkey was the industry’s favoured get-out-of jail-free technology – carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS).

The Australian government has already thrown its weight behind CCS, including special legislation to allow for offshore CO2 disposal, with virtually no evidence of its effectiveness. It is an open secret that the world’s biggest CCS project at Chevron’s Gorgon project has spectacularly failed to deliver but this has not stopped the government backing this failed technology.
Related: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected

We couldn’t even see the call for 35% electrification by 2035 be “clean” even with science clearly showing that if it’s not clean it will increase fossil gas use – adding a tenth of a degree of warming by mid-century.

Indeed, while the prime minister says every tenth of a degree of warming matters, his problem is that lowering every tenth of a degree of warming means his beloved gas industry loses more market share.
This week the WA premier, Roger Cook, jets off to Japan with gas giant Woodside – to talk up LNG markets.

title_en: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
excerpt_en: No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia
body_en: A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.

Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.

Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.

Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.

Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.

Libyan naval forces ‌rescued the vessel’s crew, the ‌sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.
Interactive Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.
The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the two drone attacks off Benghazi and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take legal and diplomatic measures against anyone found responsible.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.

HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.
On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

title_en: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
excerpt_en: District court in the Hague finds Chinese carmaker infringed on intellectual property of Jaguar Land Rover
body_en: Chinese carmaker BYD has been banned from selling its “Defender clone” vehicle in the EU by a court in the Netherlands, after Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought a case saying it infringed intellectual property rights.

JLR launched legal action over the seven-seater Ti7 SUV earlier this year after BYD announced on its website that it was taking orders from UK customers for the vehicle. Earlier this month, bailiffs acting for JLR were reported to have seized digital records from BYD’s offices.

“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover,” said the ruling from the district court in The Hague. “The characteristic ⁠and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.”

The ban will take effect one week after Friday’s ruling, which noted that BYD “currently has no concrete plans to place the Ti7 on the market in the EU”. The judge ruled, however, that the court had no jurisdiction over BYD’s activities in the UK.

BYD’s plug-in hybrid SUV, which has been on sale in China since last September, has been likened by motoring experts to the Land Rover Defender, with the BBC’s Top Gear magazine calling it the “Chinese Defender clone”.
According to BYD’s website: “An unapologetically boxy profile delivers the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look.”
Related: UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn
The Ti7 has gone on sale in the UK for £47,995, more than £20,000 cheaper than the Defender, with deliveries to customers due from January 2027.

JLR’s seven-seat Defender is one of the UK’s bestselling cars and is the company’s most popular model. The UK-based carmaker, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, sold 29,500 Defenders to retail customers between July and September this year, an increase of more than 4,000 on the same period a year earlier.
JLR said in a statement: “We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary. Legal proceedings are ongoing and we won’t be commenting further at this time.”

In a statement, BYD ⁠said it “strongly disagrees” with the ruling and will appeal. “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights,” BYD said. “We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision ⁠is incorrect.”

The court also banned BYD from producing the vehicle at its new factory at Szeged in Hungary, which is expected to start producing cars at the end of 2026, until the intellectual property case is resolved.

While many traditional carmakers have complained for some time that Chinese competitors have copied their designs, until now little has been tested in court. It is it relatively rare for European automakers to go to court over infringement of design rights.
However, JLR previously won a legal case to stop Jiangling Motors Corporation selling a copycat vehicle in 2019, after a three-year court battle.

title_en: Exquisitely decorated home of Victorian workman David Parr wins blue plaque
excerpt_en: Working-class man who covered mansions with William Morris’s patterns spent his nights filling his Cambridge terrace house with his own designs
body_en: As a Victorian working-class labourer, David Parr was paid to spend his days decorating the interiors of private mansions and Cambridge colleges with William Morris’s magnificent designs.
But as an artist, Parr chose to spend his nights filling his modest terrace house with the most resplendent decor and exquisite craftsmanship he could create.

Often working by candlelight, he spent 40 years covering his walls and ceilings with his own designs, inspired by the Morris patterns his elite clients coveted for their far grander homes and dining halls.

Yet while Morris and his wallpaper became legendary, Parr’s contributions to the Arts and Crafts movement – like those of the other skilled “art-workmen” who painted Morris’s designs – went unnoticed and overlooked.

His extraordinary home on Gwydir Street in Cambridge, which was preserved by his granddaughter Elsie throughout her lifetime, lay hidden behind an ordinary front door for more than 80 years after his death in 1927.
Now, Parr is to be honoured with a blue plaque, thought to be the first ever dedicated to a working-class Victorian art-workman.

“The Victorians used the term ‘art-workman’ for the skilled painters, carvers and craftsmen who turned designers’ ideas into finished work, usually as employees of a decorating firm,” said Annabelle Campbell, the director of the David Parr House & Gallery charity. “Their work demanded great accuracy and artistry, yet they sat at the bottom of a hierarchy of client, designer and firm, and were rarely named.”

The plaque will be unveiled on 8 February 2027, the anniversary of the day in 1886 that Parr signed the mortgage on his home, which was acquired by the charity after Elsie’s death and opened to the public in 2019.

The David Parr House, as it is now known, was discovered by accident in 2009. Tamsin Wimhurst, a social historian, knocked on 93-year-old Elsie’s door and found herself standing inside the astonishing living room of the small Victorian worker’s cottage, staring at the century-old hand-painted walls in disbelief.

“David Parr’s life was transformed by his apprenticeship and the varied and significant opportunities it opened up,” said Campbell. “As a highly skilled art-workman employed by FR Leach & Sons [a Cambridge-based decorative arts company], he was one of a class of unnamed workers who brought to reality the designs and schemes of the great figures of the Arts and Crafts movement, most notably William Morris and George Bodley.”
Yet in the records of his working life, his name appeared only as initials in a wage list, if at all, she said.
“The plaque recognises the importance of the art-workman within the successful Victorian decorative arts economy. It also recognises the vision and aspiration of a working-class family man.”

Parr spent all his free time decorating his home with designs he came up with himself, while engrossed in the work of Morris and Bodley. “He was inspired to create a house for his own family that was just as beautiful, on a smaller scale, as those he was painting.”

Many of Cambridge’s existing blue plaques honour elite academics such as Bertrand Russell and John Maynard Keynes. Campbell is proud that the new plaque will highlight the working-class heritage of the Mill Road area of the city and its important contribution to the nation’s cultural history. “Lots of these houses were occupied by highly skilled working-class Victorian artisans,” she said. “Who is commemorated with a blue plaque is changing.”

The charity is in the process of crowdfunding £6,000 to pay for a ceramic plaque to be made by a local artist, David Stonehouse, along with a short film that documents its making and an exhibition. “We don’t want to just badge the house, but to add a new layer to its history,” Campbell said. “At David Parr House, the maker, the making and the made are of equal importance and value.”

title_en: These Teachers Were Charged With Sexual Abuse. California Could Have Revoked Their Licenses Earlier but Didn’t.
excerpt_en: The post These Teachers Were Charged With Sexual Abuse. California Could Have Revoked Their Licenses Earlier but Didn’t. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Anna Vignet for ProPublica and KQED Five years before police arrested former elementary school counselor David Braff for allegedly sexually abusing students, complaints had already been sent to the state of California: that Braff had sat students on his lap, rubbed their legs and touched them near their vaginas.

But California’s educator licensing agency failed to conduct a thorough investigation after his school district reported Braff to the state in 2019. And the agency allowed Braff to continue working with children. It wasn’t until his 2024 arrest that the agency suspended his credentials. By then, he’d gotten jobs at three more Southern California schools. At one of them, prosecutors allege, another student complained the guidance counselor had touched him, too.

The state Commission on Teacher Credentialing also delayed revoking the credentials of two other teachers who were later convicted of sexually abusing students. As with Braff, schools had reported those educators to the agency that determines who can work in California’s public schools. And as with Braff, the commission allowed those teachers to keep teaching — and draw new complaints — until after they were criminally charged, an investigation by KQED and ProPublica found. That includes a middle school math teacher who sent his student a video showing a boy’s genitals and an elementary teacher who touched students’ butts and vaginal areas and placed their hands on his crotch, according to court records.

In each of the cases, state investigators did not interview some of the students who had alleged abuse, according to the students, parents and attorneys who spoke to KQED and ProPublica. Several former agency staffers, including investigators, told the news outlets that, at times, the volunteer panel tasked with assessing teacher accusations overlooked evidence of wrongdoing. That perspective from staff members was backed up by two former members of the panel and two people who served on the state commission that ultimately decides teacher discipline.

After police arrested Braff in 2024, a parent emailed Jeffrey Weinstein, superintendent at Santa Paula Unified School District, where Braff was first accused of sexually abusing students. “Who dropped the ball and allowed this monster to still be around kids?” the parent wrote, according to public records obtained by the news outlets. (Weinstein was not working at Santa Paula at the time students accused Braff.)

In his emailed response, Weinstein blamed the state’s teacher licensing agency. He told the parent that the district had conducted its own investigation and reported the guidance counselor to the state as well as to police. He also said he had reviewed the district’s investigative file and “vehemently disagreed” with the agency’s decision not to revoke Braff’s credentials.
“We sent all the evidence we had gathered,” Weinstein said. “The district did everything in its legal capacity it could.”

Braff is soon to stand trial for sexually abusing 15 students, including 13 from Santa Paula. He has been in jail since November 2024. He has pleaded not guilty and did not respond to a request for comment sent through the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office’s electronic messaging system. His attorney declined to comment.

Braff had previously told Santa Paula Unified administrators that he did not touch students near their private parts or have them sit on his lap — and that he only gave students side hugs, high-fives, fist bumps and taps on the knee, according to the district’s 2019 report to the state.

“Mr. Braff described keeping an office environment where kids can move around; and he would not be closer than arm’s length,” the report said, summarizing the district’s interview with Braff. “It was not his intent to make them afraid but rather feel that there was someone in their corner; someone to talk to.”

The Santa Paula Unified School District recognized guidance counselor David Braff as employee of the month in 2017. The district reported him to the state for misconduct two years later. Santa Paula Unified School District via Facebook Anita Fitzhugh, a spokesperson for the Commission on Teacher Credentialing, said the state automatically revokes teachers’ credentials when they are convicted of sexual criminal offenses. But she wrote in a statement that “unless the applicant or educator is convicted of a mandatory criminal offense, there are no written criteria that set the level of adverse action for educator discipline matters.” She did not answer questions about specific cases or details of the investigative process.

Fitzhugh said the state does not provide any guidelines for those reviewing teacher misconduct cases about when discipline is warranted or the type of punishment that should be meted out. And she said it was the commission’s role to balance “protecting students as well as the legal rights of educators who have been accused but not convicted.”

California’s system of disciplining educators dates to the 1970s, Fitzhugh said, and “a deep and comprehensive review of the educator discipline system, prioritizing student safety in the schools, is in order.”
“We expect the Commission to take this up in the near future,” she said.

Students Not Interviewed In the summer of 2019, California’s Commission on Teacher Credentialing received a detailed report from the Santa Paula school district about Braff’s alleged misconduct at McKevett Elementary School. The state requires districts to report educators when they resign or are fired after allegations of misconduct. Braff, who had been a guidance counselor at the school for four years, had resigned in the midst of the district’s investigation into complaints by at least seven students that he had touched them inappropriately.

title_en: Burundi’s refugees are under pressure to return: why some choose silence when they do
excerpt_en: Silence is a way through which Burundians navigate political uncertainty.
body_en: Burundi has experienced repeated cycles of political violence and displacement, notably following the assassination of President Melchior Ndadayé in 1993. Further unrest followed during an election-related political crisis in 2015.

These cycles of unrest have resulted in thousands of deaths and forced hundreds of thousands of Burundians to flee their country. Over the past two decades, more than 1.1 million have sought refuge in other countries, primarily in neighbouring Tanzania. Others have fled to Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and further.

There’s growing pressure from the Burundian state, as well as from neighbouring host countries, including Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya, to encourage repatriation. This reflects a broader regional shift in which the continued presence of Burundian refugees outside their country is becoming increasingly conditional.

Indeed, under international initiatives led by the UN refugee agency, Burundi has established a formal policy framework for repatriation. But return to contexts of forced displacement, violence and other forms of persecution has prompted questions about whether it can work and how it is experienced by those who return.

My doctoral research examines the governance of return migration, specifically its long-term implications for returnees. In a recent article, I explore the experience of Burundian returnees, drawing on 23 interviews with returnees, focus group discussions, and participant observation conducted in Burundi in 2024 and 2025.

My research shows that return to “post-crisis” Burundi is much more than a physical or administrative process. It is a politicised action within the country’s history of conflicts and repeated displacement. I found that returnees were typically evasive about life in exile and chose their words carefully, so as not to give away too much about themselves.

Their silence proposes, in its own way, an alternative account of return. It is an account that unsettles official narratives of “successful” return, reintegration and stability, and insists on the unresolved tensions that continue to structure life in Burundi.

Return by all means Voluntary repatriation has been on Burundi’s policy agenda for decades. Burundi and Tanzania first agreed to a tripartite mechanism for refugee repatriation in 1998, with the support of the UN. The agreement has since been reactivated, most recently in December 2025. Between January and August 2026 alone, 96,602 refugees returned from Tanzania, and Nduta and Nyarugusu refugee camps were progressively closed.

Officials on both sides have portrayed this “acceleration” of return as a success story. Burundian authorities have repeatedly framed returns as evidence of restored stability, constructing the country as a “ safe zone ” to reinforce its political legitimacy.

In practice, however, return has been shaped less by voluntariness than by a combination of incentives and constraints. In Tanzania, authorities have taken measures to deter new arrivals and encourage refugee returns. They have reduced humanitarian aid, limited access to healthcare and education, and carried out forced repatriation. This questions the character of these “voluntary” returns, and highlights their coercive nature.
Several factors complicate the prospect of return as a lasting solution, including:
limited access to employment, housing and essential services
concerns about deteriorating human rights
Return under a political cloud My paper draws on field research in two sites: the borderland province of Muyinga, one of Burundi’s largest return destinations; and Bujumbura Mairie, the capital.

Interviews reveal that return has become more politically charged, particularly since the 2015 political crisis, which triggered renewed displacement and intensified political repression. Returnees affiliated with opposition movements or particular ethnic factions may attract suspicion or surveillance and face fears for their safety, depending on where and when they were exiled.
My research shows how silence provides space to navigate life upon return.

Some returnees were evasive, carefully managing who to tell about their displacement, and who not to tell. One returnee confided his 2015 flight to a Tutsi friend while in exile, but swore him to secrecy, while avoiding the subject entirely with fellow Hutus. He felt they might ask why he left “when we stayed to defend our country”.

For some, perceptions were informed less by who they were than by where they had been. They recalled that those who stayed behind could never be sure whether returnees had come back as “the Burundians they had once known”, or had returned changed, implicated in rebellion or sent back to destabilise the country.
Others described forms of concealment centred on identity. One second-generation returnee adjusted her own accent so that she wouldn’t sound like an outsider.
These forms of silence are about navigating political uncertainty and negotiating a place within an evolving social and political order.

Silence, in this sense, can itself be a form of political agency. In selecting what aspects of their experience to disclose, to whom, and in what context, returnees are not simply protecting themselves. They are shaping the terms on which their experience enters public life at all.

Understanding post-return The experiences of Burundian returnees show that silence is not simply an absence of speech, but an active practice through which experiences of displacement are continuously negotiated.

title_en: A new Democratic Congress will view Trump’s harsh Cuba policy skeptically – but that doesn’t mean a change is coming soon
excerpt_en: Cuba is unlikely to be a huge priority for incoming Democrats, and the Trump administration is unlikely to change its maximum pressure approach.
body_en: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has designs for Cuba – and potentially on the U.S. presidency. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images The so-called “ blue tsunami ” that hit the United States in the midterm elections is causing ripples around the world.
Having won a historic victory, congressional Democrats now appear poised to challenge the Trump administration’s conduct of foreign affairs.
The Iran war, support for Ukraine and the management of Venezuelan oil certainly all appear to be on the agenda of some Democrats.
The flipping of the House and Senate from Republican to Democratic control has also led to speculation that members of Congress may also wish to challenge Trump’s Cuba policy.

After all, the United States’ position on Cuba has swung in recent decades, depending on the balance of power in Washington. An easing of tensions and normalization of relations between the U.S. and Cuba took place under the presidency of Barack Obama, only to be reversed following the election of Donald Trump in 2016. President Joe Biden largely followed Trump’s lead, while making more allowance for activities supporting the Cuban people.

In his second term, however, Trump has pursued an even harder line than before. Since January 2026, the administration has instituted a devastating economic and fuel blockade, prohibiting Cubans from importing oil. This pressure tactic is meant to get the Cuban government to agree to increased economic privatization and political democratization.

A man walks in the dark during a blackout in Cuba on Sept. 18, 2026. AP Photo/Ramon Espinosa While the Cuban government has met certain demands, notably with respect to the economy, it has resolutely refused to change either its personnel or its authoritarian character.
The result of this blockade has been a stalemate and increased hardship for Cubans. As a historian of U.S.-Cuban relations, I saw that hardship firsthand during a visit to Havana in June 2026.

While I understand the notion that emboldened Democrats may try to force a change in direction of the Trump administration’s foreign policy, including on Cuba, I doubt they will be able to do so. In fact, there are reasons to believe that the midterm results may actually reinforce Republicans’ hard-line approach to the Caribbean island.
Strained life in Cuba Since 1961, at the height of the Cold War, the U.S. government has enforced a rigorous sanctions regime against communist Cuba – the longest-running embargo in modern history.

In January 2026, the Trump administration made that embargo even more severe with the oil importation ban, part of a regional pressure campaign that also saw U.S. forces abduct and remove from office Venezuela’s President Nicolás Maduro, a longtime ally of the Cuban government.
For Cubans, no oil means no electricity. Blackouts, already a problem, have become longer and more frequent.

Absent electricity, Cubans have no regular access to running water. Disease, from mosquitoes, other pests and unsafe water, has increased dramatically. Cuba’s once much-praised medical system often cannot treat patients unless they bring their own drugs and supplies.
Inflation has soared and tourists have stopped coming, while industrial and agricultural production has declined dramatically.

Cubans hate the U.S. embargo for contributing to this misery. At the same time, many also blame their government. During my last visit, Cubans I spoke with told me that they believe their leaders are more concerned with protecting their power and privileges than with the welfare of the average Cuban.
For many Cubans, this indifference explains why President Miguel Díaz-Canel and his allies have rejected the Trump administration’s central demand of surrendering their monopoly on power.
Havana’s strategy Trump’s demands, blockade and the threat of military force have led to some concessions by Cuba’s leaders.
During the past year, Cuba’s government has released some political prisoners and permitted greater foreign investment, most notably from Cuban Americans.
Blackouts are a part of life in Havana. Yamil Lage/AFP via Getty Images The government in Havana has also expanded the range of legally permitted private enterprise in Cuba.

But when it comes to the question of power, Díaz-Canel and his allies remain implacable. They know that relinquishing power will cut off the supply of profits from state-owned businesses that flows their way and maintains their opulent lifestyles.
They also argue that Trump has no right to determine the rulers of a sovereign nation.
Rubio’s ideological priority For the moment, it appears that Díaz-Canel hopes international and domestic politics will compel Trump to turn his attention from Cuba.

title_en: The Binance hack exploited familiar weaknesses – all organisations should learn from it
excerpt_en: The hackers compromised a laptop belonging to an IT engineer, according to Binance.
body_en: Hackers have stolen around US$6.3 billion (£4.7 billion) from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, most of which was taken in under an hour. According to Binance, the attack exploited systems and individuals with the authority to carry out transactions involving such large sums.

Such vulnerabilities exist everywhere; statistics show that people and the systems they directly use, including their personal computers, remain a top target for cybercriminals. All organisations could therefore learn lessons from this attack.

The Binance theft took place on the evening of October 29, 2026. The Binance attack netted four times the amount stolen in the previous biggest cryptocurrency theft, on the Bybit exchange in February 2025.

Private keys, used to authorise spending or withdrawal from crypto-wallets, are a known vulnerability. But Binance found no evidence these were leaked. An initial statement from the exchange pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. This gave the attacker access to the internal system that processes withdrawal requests.

Because blockchain transactions can be fully audited, investigators can trace the events leading up to the attack. On October 28, the address from which the theft was later carried out received 0.3 ETH (Ether cryptocurrency) from Tornado Cash, a service that mixes funds from multiple users to hide their origin.

A few hours before the theft, a malicious smart contract (computer code that automatically runs when certain conditions are met) was deployed from the same address. At 20:20:59 UTC, a transaction was sent from that address containing 50 signed authorisations intended to transfer control of a Binance wallet to that smart contract. One of them was accepted by a Binance hot wallet (a wallet used by the exchange to process customer withdrawals).

Following this takeover, the hackers proceeded to empty the hot wallet of 64 different tokens worth approximately $2.5 billion (£1.8 billion) in a single transaction. Other wallets were then emptied in parallel using standard signed transactions, bringing the total amount stolen to $6.3 billion. Valid Binance digital signatures were needed for draining the wallets, but how the attackers obtained these has not been explained.
The same audit trail shows that the attackers were rehearsing several hours earlier, but at that stage, nothing linked them to Binance.

Familiar tactics The 2025 attack on Bybit, which resulted in the theft of US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion), also appears to have involved a compromised laptop that was capable of performing operations requiring high-level privileges.

North Korean cybercriminals, who were implicated in the attack on the Bybit exchange by analysts, specialise in creating so-called “legends”. These are identities created to deceive companies and individuals. In October, the US Department of Justice indicted 14 individuals in a case in which North Korean cybercriminals, using stolen or fabricated identities, secured remote jobs at more than 70 US companies.

As of Sunday November 1, Binance had restored withdrawals for certain cryptocurrencies. Chinnapong / Shutterstock Two days before the attack, Binance reported that, for a week, it had been blocking North Korea-linked attack attempts involving fake recruiters. Was this related to the attack? We don’t know yet, but the modus operandi is well recognised and widespread. North Korea, meanwhile, has denied allegations that it was behind the attack.

A cybercriminal can use a legend to pose for months as a hardworking employee, a cheap and reliable contractor, or as a generous employer. The criminal waits for the moment when a crucial software installation is carried out or a vital document is signed. Since a large amount of today’s work involves only digital interactions with people, it is sensible to approach every new contact with limited trust.

A good example of how such legends work is the attack on the Japanese DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024, which netted US$308 million (£230 million) for the attackers. The hacker posed as a recruiter on LinkedIn and gained the trust of a Ginco employee.

Compromised laptops may have played a role in several cryptocurrency attacks. Aldabra Studio / Shutterstock Ginco is a company that provides DMM with wallet management software. The recruiter offered the Ginco employee a job on the condition that they completed a recruitment test. The test URL actually led to a malicious Python script; from this point on, the victim’s computer was compromised.
This is classic social engineering. In this case, the target was a cryptocurrency wallet system accessed through a compromised computer. About two months later, the attackers drained funds from DMM.

Lessons for business Virtually all businesses should learn from such attacks. The first lesson concerns what their computer systems are allowed to authorise. Traditionally, cryptographic keys are protected using devices known as hardware security modules and multi-signature schemes (where multiple private keys are required to authorise an action).

Unfortunately, such mechanisms do not protect against an attack launched from a compromised internal system controlled by a hacker. It is advisable to define rules for authorising financial transactions, set time and amount limits, and require approval via an alternative channel for unusual requests.

Additionally, since most of the funds in the Binance cyberattack were transferred within an hour, computer systems should have mechanisms in place to block suspicious transactions within seconds, without waiting for approval from the on-duty security engineer.

The second lesson is about recruitment, which has evolved into a security mechanism. North Korean cybercriminals use stolen or fabricated identities and virtual private networks (VPNs) to pose as people living in the US.

Visual identities during online interviews can be falsified using deepfakes. Video interviews and CVs no longer prove who someone really is. In some cases, actors are even hired for in-person interviews. Today, we need to focus on strengthening the identity verification process. It’s important to check candidates through independently verified contacts during this process.
